turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Monday, September 7. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex. Germany had an election this weekend, and it's not a small one.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The AfD just won Saxony-Anhalt outright — 43.8% in Saturday's state election, more than double the CDU's 17.2%.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 39 of 83 seats, 3 short of an outright majority, but it's the first time the AfD has had a real shot at leading a state government. It's a direct rebuke of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does a state win actually translate into governing power, or is this mostly symbolic given Germany's firewall against coalitions with the AfD?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: On paper the firewall holds — every mainstream party has ruled out a coalition. But holding 44% of a state electorate changes the incentive math heading toward 2029, and every mainstream party now has to answer for why it isn't governing with the largest bloc.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Miami next. An Amazon Prime Air cargo jet — a Boeing 767 — overran the runway at Miami International Saturday night, inbound from San Juan.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 5 dead, 5 injured, 3 of them critical. It struck ground vehicles and caught fire. NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy already has a team on site — and because 21 Air flies that route under contract to Amazon's cargo network, whatever the investigation finds about maintenance or crew procedure could ripple straight into how Amazon audits every contracted operator flying under its brand, not just this one aircraft.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And in Ohio — a man carrying a taser and two pistols lunged at Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton at the Canfield Fair Saturday.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Patrick Havas, 38, is facing disorderly conduct and two assault counts. Acton wasn't hurt, several bystanders were, and the condemnation's been bipartisan — even her Republican rival's campaign called it out. It lands in a midterm cycle where state-level campaign security has already been an open worry, not a one-off scare.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: US business. Uber's cutting 3,300 jobs — 10% of the workforce, its biggest cut since the pandemic.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Khosrowshahi's cutting management layers 20%, small teams in half, and capping remote work at 1% of staff. Wedbush pegs the savings around $1.75 billion, all reinvested into rideshare, delivery, and robotaxi.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Robotaxi's the tell there, isn't it — this reads less like belt-tightening and more like funding the Waymo fight.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the read. Uber isn't retrenching, it's reallocating — cutting headcount now to fund the capital-intensive autonomous pivot before margins get squeezed from both directions at once.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Campbell's is cutting about 515 salaried roles and closing 2 snack plants, chasing $500 million in savings by fiscal 2030.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Fiscal-year sales came in at $9.7 billion, down 5%, as shoppers keep trading down to private label. Price hikes are coming on 60% of the portfolio, and CEO Beekhuizen didn't dress it up — called the results "unacceptable." That's a packaged-food company raising prices into weak volume at the same time, which only works if the private-label defection has actually bottomed — a bet Campbell's is making without much evidence yet that it has.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: International. Bolivia's government just seized control of its own state oil company.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Supreme Decree 5699 puts YPFB and the fuel regulator under a 180-day government intervention, extendable another 90. The energy minister's alleging corruption networks inside and outside the fuel supply chain — this after months of diesel and gasoline shortages.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is nationalizing your own national oil company an admission the original model failed?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Pretty much. YPFB's been the delivery mechanism for the shortages, not just a victim of them — stripping its marketing role entirely is the tell. They're not fixing management, they're routing around it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And Kenya — the central bank cleared South Africa's Nedbank to take up to 66% of NCBA Group, after shareholders tendered nearly 80% of shares.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Kenya's now Africa's top M&A market by value in the first half — $1.44 billion, up 671% year on year, overtaking Nigeria. Worth watching whether that capital keeps rotating east or this is a one-deal spike — a single cross-border bank acquisition that size can flatter a half-year table on its own.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Markets — quick one today, US desks are shut for Labor Day, so this is Friday's close.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And it was a quiet tape by our threshold — S&P off 0.38%, Nasdaq off 0.29%, Dow down 0.51%, nothing worth reading a full board of numbers for. It's all on the Markets tab if you want it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The one thing that did move the tape — the August jobs report. 162,000 added against roughly 55,000 expected, unemployment steady at 4.1%.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That single print flipped the rate conversation. Fed funds futures went from pricing a cut this month to pricing something like a 52 to 58% chance of a hike. The 10-year added about 3 basis points, gold slipped just over 1%, the dollar firmed.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the "good news is bad news" dynamic is back.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Squarely. A labor market that strong argues the Fed doesn't need to rescue growth, which argues against the cut the market had been leaning on. The one place that repricing landed hardest wasn't even a US asset — it's the peso, fresh record low against the dollar, fifth record close in six sessions. We'll get to why that matters beyond FX in a bit. WTI's up nearly 10% on the week too, but that's Hormuz risk compounding, not a Friday move — worth flagging, not worth a full segment.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One thing under the index headline worth a line — Russell 2000 was actually up 0.25% while the majors slipped.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Small breadth divergence, and it fits the jobs-report read — small caps skew more domestically levered, so a strong labor print that argues for a resilient US economy is a small-cap-friendly signal even when it's a large-cap-unfriendly one for rate-sensitive growth names. Not a story on its own, just the kind of detail that tells you the tape's more nuanced than the three headline indices suggest.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Deep Dive today is a Supreme Court ruling, and it's a strange one — the Chief Justice broke with his own bloc.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Late last week, the Court ruled 5 to 4 to let the White House's ballroom construction — the East Wing demolition — proceed without congressional appropriation or National Capital Planning Commission review. Roberts dissented. Not with Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, or Barrett — with the three Democratic appointees.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a genuinely unusual lineup for a presidential-power case.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It is. Roberts called it "likely unlawful," and his argument is structural, not aesthetic — he's saying the executive branch just got permission to bypass Congress's power of the purse and its constitutional authority over federal property in DC, by simply not asking. No appropriation, no NCPC sign-off, no statutory review. He cites Theodore Roosevelt and Churchill on why the capital's architecture belongs to the public, not to whoever's occupying the residence.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the actual legal mechanism the majority used to get around that review requirement, versus just asserting the power?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The majority's theory leans on inherent executive authority over the White House complex as the president's own workspace — treating NCPC review and appropriations process as advisory rather than binding when it's the president's own residence being modified. That's the part Roberts is flagging as dangerous — not this ballroom specifically, but the precedent that "it's my house" beats a statutory review process whenever the executive decides it does.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why does a sitting Chief Justice publicly split from every other Republican appointee on the Court to say that?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because Roberts has spent two decades building his legacy around institutional process — the idea that even when the Court reaches a conservative outcome, it should reach it through the right channel. This ruling doesn't just decide a ballroom. It sets a template: any future administration facing a review process it doesn't like can point to "presidential workspace" as the workaround. That's a bypass mechanism sitting right next to a bunch of other bypasses this week — a utility building around its own interconnection queue, a market refusing to believe a genuinely strong earnings number. Everyone's finding a way around the process that's supposed to slow them down.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does the ruling actually stop the demolition, or is that already done?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The East Wing's already down — this ruling just closes off the legal challenge that might have forced remediation or a redo through proper channels. So functionally, the precedent matters more going forward than the building does now. Watch whether Congress tries to legislate the NCPC's authority into something harder to route around — that's the next move in this fight, and it's a slower one than a demolition crew.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is this actually a partisan precedent, or does it cut both ways for whoever holds the White House next?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the part that should worry both sides equally, and it's probably why Roberts broke ranks. "Presidential workspace" as a review-bypass doesn't come with a party label attached to it — a Democratic administration in 2029 inherits the exact same argument for anything it wants to build, demolish, or convert inside the complex without asking Congress or the planning commission first. Roberts is playing a longer game than this one ballroom; he's trying to stop a precedent that every future occupant of the office would love to have and none of them should.

segments.raw: SEGMENT FOUR — ENERGY / DATA CENTERS / UTILITIES
segments.label: Energy / Data Centers / Utilities

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Energy desk. Something in your inbox this week that's a genuine queue-bypass story, not just another interconnection headline.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: PG&E's "Flex Connect" program. It's a flexible, curtailable interconnection track that lets large distribution-connected loads energize in months instead of the multi-year firm-interconnection queue — in exchange for letting PG&E curtail them when the system's constrained.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the actual hit rate on capacity under that trade-off? Because "we might curtail you" is a real risk for anyone sizing a load.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the number that makes this interesting — customers still got their needed capacity in 90% of hours across the pilot's first two years. PG&E's had 10 Flex Connect applications from large-load customers in 2026 alone, a sharp jump, and the pipeline's shifted from mostly EV charging into smaller data centers and battery storage.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How's that different from what PJM and MISO have already done on curtailable and computational load?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: PJM's ride-through rules and MISO's computational-load classification are both about managing risk on load that's already interconnected. Flex Connect is upstream of that — it's a queue-bypass mechanism, letting you skip years of firm-interconnection study entirely if you accept curtailment terms up front. For a developer trying to site a mid-size campus fast, that's a fundamentally different negotiation than waiting in line — you're trading certainty of full capacity for speed to power, and the 90% figure is what makes that trade actually underwritable instead of a leap of faith.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: There's also a lawsuit in your notes — California versus the Trump administration over an offshore wind lease.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: California's AG and Energy Commission sued over a forced buyback of a 2-gigawatt offshore lease off the central coast, alleging Interior tanked the lease's value and then extended what the suit calls an "unrefusable" $150 million buyout. It's the same playbook Interior used in March — paying TotalEnergies $928 million to relinquish 4.2 gigawatts of leases off North Carolina and New York.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So it's becoming a pattern, not a one-off policy call.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Two data points is early for "pattern," but it's now a repeatable model — devalue the asset through permitting friction, then make an offer the developer can't refuse. Worth watching if a third one shows up before we call it policy. And it's the same underwriting problem we keep coming back to on this show — whoever holds an offtake or a lease has to now price in the risk that the counterparty isn't the market, it's the federal government deciding your asset's worth less than you paid for it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Last one — Santee Cooper and Google, which is the AI story running in the opposite direction from usual.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right, this isn't AI as a load driver, it's AI as the capex-planning tool. Santee Cooper's using Google's WeatherNext 2 model for probabilistic load forecasting — hundreds of ensemble scenarios in under a minute, 15-day lead times — feeding straight into daily dispatch decisions, plus a Gemini agent doing scenario planning against its own $10 billion grid-expansion budget. Cuts scenario-run time up to 75%. NextEra's doing something parallel. Worth remembering that half of this decade's AI buildout is also quietly rebuilding the tools utilities use to plan for it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does faster scenario planning actually change a grid-expansion budget, or is it just the same $10 billion spent more efficiently?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: In the near term it's efficiency — better-targeted capex within the same envelope. But the real value is optionality: a utility that can re-run 15-day load scenarios in under a minute can react to a large-load interconnection request, a heat wave, or a generation outage inside the planning cycle instead of waiting for the next quarterly forecast update. That's the same instinct behind PG&E's Flex Connect — both are utilities building faster decision loops because the old cadence, built for slow, predictable load growth, doesn't match a world where a single data-center campus can show up wanting gigawatts on a compressed timeline.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Bago tayo pumunta sa Pilipinas, dalawang salita muna, at Tagalog lang, walang Ingles.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Sige. Unang salita: huwad. Ibig sabihin, peke o hindi totoo — pero mas mabigat ang dating nito kaysa sa "peke" sa usual na pag-uusap, kasi ginagamit ito pag mismong pagkakakilanlan ng isang tao ang tinatanong, hindi lang basta produkto.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Kaya bang gamitin sa pang-araw-araw, o pormal lang talaga ito, panlegal o pambalita?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Puwede sa dalawa — pero mas madalas mo itong maririnig sa balita o sa korte kaysa sa kusina. May kapatid itong salita na "peke," na mas kaswal, at "impostor" kung tao mismo ang tinutukoy. Ang "huwad" ay nasa gitna — pormal na sapat para sa testimonya, pero hindi ganoon kalayo sa karaniwang salita kaya naiintindihan agad ng lahat.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Pangalawang salita naman.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Paghihiwalay. Ugat nito ang "hiwalay," at ang paghihiwalay ay ang proseso ng paghahati — hindi lang basta away, kundi aktwal na pagkakawatak-watak ng isang grupo o alyansa na dating iisa.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: May pagkakaiba ba ito sa "hidwaan," na madalas ding gamit pag may away sa pulitika?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Malaki ang pagkakaiba. Ang hidwaan ay ang alitan mismo — ang tunggalian. Ang paghihiwalay ay ang resulta nito kapag talagang naghiwalay na ang mga panig, hindi na basta nag-aaway kundi magkahiwalay na ang landas. Isasama natin ang dalawang salitang ito sa balita ngayon tungkol sa Pilipinas.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Bago tayo lumipat, madalas ba talagang gamitin ang dalawang salitang ito sa totoong balitaan, o mas madalas lang sa akademya?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Talagang gamit na gamit sa balitaan, lalo na ngayon — dahil pareho itong tumutukoy sa mga sitwasyon kung saan may itinatago o may nagkakawatak-watak. Kapag pinag-usapan ang huwad na mga pangalan sa listahan ng pondo, o ang paghihiwalay ng isang partido mula sa dating kasama nito, ito mismo ang tamang salita — hindi basta-basta, kundi eksaktong tumutugma sa nangyayari.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: At doon na nga tayo — Araw 22 ng paglilitis kay dating Bise Presidente Duterte, at may inamin ang depensa ngayong araw.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tinestigo ng PSA na 152 lamang sa 2,669 umanong tatanggap ng confidential funds ang tumugma sa civil registry — 37 sa mga tumugma ay may death record, 25 ay wala pang 16 anyos. Sa huli, inamin ng abogado ng depensa na si Justin Gular na ang mga pangalang ito ay huwad — mga alyas — at tinawag niya itong "classified information."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Right — that's the alias admission the prosecution's calling an 11th-hour reversal. It confirms months of skepticism about the payee list in a single line on the record.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly, and it puts more weight on what Senator-judge Tulfo's been pushing for — Colonels Lachica and Nolasco actually testifying about who compiled that list in the first place.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ang piso naman, bumagsak ulit sa bagong record low na 62.59 kada dolyar noong Biyernes — ika-5 sunod-sunod na record sa loob ng 6 na araw ng kalakalan.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And there's a new data point behind that beyond just dollar strength — the Philippines' gross international reserves fell to an 18-month low of $103.317 billion as of July, which narrows how much room the BSP actually has to defend the peso through direct intervention. BusinessWorld's flagging further downside risk if the Fed really does lean toward a hike, and remember, that's the exact same US jobs-report repricing we just walked through in the market segment — it's not a coincidence, it's the transmission mechanism, showing up first in the currency with the least room to absorb it. And no PSEi line today — the index didn't move enough to earn one.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One more, a week out — the first-ever Bangsamoro Parliament election, September 14. 80 seats, 2.3 million registered voters, over 600 candidates.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And it's genuinely competitive, which BARMM elections haven't really been before. The MILF's own party, the UBJP under Murad Ebrahim, is facing an unexpected paghihiwalay from within its own coalition — a breakaway Bangsamoro Federalist Party linked to Marcos's own party, running 74 candidates against the UBJP's 81. The MILF and the government's peace office signed a security-cooperation pact ahead of the vote, which tells you how seriously both sides are taking a split nobody expected two years ago.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two Mandarin words before China, both HSK-4 level, both aimed at exactly the gap in your Mandarin — connectives and abstract collocations rather than nouns.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: First: 只要…就… — zhǐyào... jiù... It's "as long as... then..." — a conditional connective, more formal-leaning than "如果...就...", and it implies a sufficient condition, not just any condition. Example: 只要经济不回暖，股市就难以起色。("As long as the economy doesn't warm up, the stock market will struggle to recover.")

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How does that differ from 如果, which most learners get taught first?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 如果 is neutral — "if X, then Y," any hypothetical. 只要 specifically frames X as the one sufficient condition — it's saying "this alone is enough to guarantee Y," which is a stronger, more analytical claim. You'll hear it constantly in finance and policy speech because it's built for exactly that kind of argument.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second word.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 脱节 — tuōjié. Literally "to come apart at the joint," used abstractly to mean disconnected, out of sync. It's 书面语, more formal register — you wouldn't use it for "my phone's disconnected," you'd use it for two things that should move together but no longer do. Example: 利润增长与股市表现脱节。("Profit growth has become disconnected from stock-market performance.") That's actually today's China story.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Any near-synonym worth contrasting there?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 分离 — fēnlí — means separated too, but it's more physical or literal, like two objects pulled apart. 脱节 is specifically for a relationship or correlation that's broken down between two things that are supposed to track each other. That's the nuance — and it's exactly the word for the story we're about to get into.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Can you actually combine the two words in one sentence, the way a fluent speaker would in a finance context?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Sure — 只要投资者不信任利润数字，估值就会继续脱节。("As long as investors don't trust the profit numbers, valuations will keep staying disconnected from them.") That's a natural finance-desk sentence, and it's almost exactly the argument we're about to make about China.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: China, and it's the two-speed story turned inward on the market itself this time.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 利润增长与股市表现脱节。Profit growth has become disconnected from stock-market performance. Onshore-listed company profits climbed 25.7% year on year in Q2 — the fastest pace in nearly 5 years, per CICC — and H1 net profit across listed firms hit 3.58 trillion yuan, around $528 billion, up 19.5%.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And yet the market's doing the opposite.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Completely the opposite. The CSI 300's down about 9% this quarter, and the STAR 50 — the tech-heavy board — has fallen 29%. 只要经济不回暖，股市就难以起色, as the saying goes: as long as the broader economy doesn't actually warm up, the market won't either, no matter what one earnings print says.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So investors are pricing the macro backdrop and the AI-capex payoff question over the actual company-level numbers.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the read. A profit number that strong would normally re-rate a market — instead it's getting shrugged off, because nobody trusts it'll persist against a still-weak property sector and open doubts about whether AI capex is generating returns anywhere close to what's been spent. When the print and the price stop agreeing, the price is usually the one expressing what the market actually believes.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is there a specific company showing that gap in real time, not just the index-level numbers?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Vanke's the sharper version of it. The developer deferred quarterly bank-loan interest to annual payments in a rescue the Shenzhen state-asset regulator brokered with four state banks — and every one of those deferred payments comes due this month. It's got more than 9.4 billion yuan in bonds maturing over the next 6 months on top of that. That's the same extend-and-pretend logic as the local-government debt swap we covered a few weeks back, just now landing at a single company with a real, dated deadline instead of a policy abstraction.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Arts. Virginia Museum of Fine Arts just put out an acquisitions report that's a different model from the usual single-trophy-lot story.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 808 purchases plus 2,506 gifts from over 50 donors, across all 10 curatorial departments, in the past year alone. The headline piece is Adam Pendleton and Jaune Quick-to-See Smith's "Making Medicine: Coyote," a canoe-form sculpture now installed in the museum's Waterways gallery.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How does that compare to the National Gallery's 190-work haul we covered a couple weeks back?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Different model entirely. The NGA move was one big lot, one moment. This is a mid-tier encyclopedic museum using its whole machinery — every department, dozens of donors — to build depth quietly rather than chase a single headline. Quick-to-See Smith, who died in 2023, keeps racking up posthumous acquisitions like this; worth watching if that becomes the template as blue-chip contemporary prices push museums like VMFA further out of the primary market.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: In opera — a genuinely American premiere, and not a European import for once.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "A River Runs Through It," composer Zach Redler adapting Norman Maclean's novella, world premiere at the Ellen Theatre in Bozeman on September 18, timed to the book's 50th anniversary. The score folds in bluegrass, country, jazz, and honky-tonk rather than a conventional classical frame — a direct counterpoint to the Lili Elbe piece we covered closing in Santa Fe, which was very much the European-import model.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And one in literature — a mid-career reassessment rather than a new release.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Paris Review ran a piece by Luke Dunne on poet Dorothea Lasky — 10 collections in, including one built around "The Shining" and a forthcoming Sappho project, plus a nonfiction collection that ranges from fashion criticism to Satanism to David Hockney. It's a marker of where criticism's attention is drifting: back toward confessional, occult-adjacent poets who built cult followings outside the prize circuit, rather than toward whoever's shortlisted this season.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Op-eds. Mohamed El-Erian's got a piece making the rounds arguing the AI trade's about to get bumpier.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: His case: AI diffusion has been broad but shallow — it hasn't penetrated deep enough into actual workflows to justify the financing pouring into it. Hyperscalers have sold about $500 billion in bonds this year and plan to borrow at least $300 billion more by year-end, which puts them competing directly with the Treasury for capital just as both US parties turn populist on Big Tech. His prescription is more government-industry coordination to manage the transition.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Steelman aside — where does that argument actually fall apart?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The circularity he ducks. If the productivity gains really are as shallow as he says, "more coordination" doesn't fix a capital structure where debt service is outrunning realized cash flow — that's a math problem, not a communication problem. And he never actually answers who eats the loss if the financing gap doesn't close on its own. That's the same open question that's been running through this show all week — Georgia Power's exit-cost socialization, Venezuela's hundred-year concessions, now hyperscaler bond math. Somebody always eats it; the op-ed just doesn't say who.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What would real "coordination" even look like in practice, beyond a vague call for it?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Probably some version of what utilities already do with ratepayers — spreading the financing risk across a broader base so no single balance sheet is fully exposed if the AI-ROI case comes in soft. The problem is nobody's proposed who that broader base is for a hyperscaler's bond book the way a ratebase exists for a utility's. Until someone answers that, "coordination" is a placeholder for a mechanism that doesn't exist yet.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second piece — Anne Krueger on shipbuilding protectionism.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Her argument: a century of Jones Act-style protection left US shipbuilding globally uncompetitive, and the new round of tariffs and subsidies aimed at reviving it will fail the same way — protection raises costs for shippers without building real capacity.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the counter?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Her free-trade framework assumes shipbuilding should be judged like any other industry, where comparative advantage should just win. But the administration's actual argument isn't efficiency — it's sealift and national-security capacity, a Pentagon concern, not a market one. "A hundred years of protection failed" is a real indictment of the old approach. It's not proof that a better-targeted industrial policy couldn't work over a longer build-out horizon. She's arguing against a strategy nobody serious is actually proposing.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is there a version of targeted industrial policy that actually addresses her underlying point about cost?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Probably one that ties subsidy to measurable output — cost-per-ton, delivery timelines, actual capacity added — rather than open-ended protection with no sunset clause, which is closer to what the Jones Act became. Krueger's right that unconditional protection breeds exactly the complacency she describes. Where she overreaches is treating that as proof the whole category of intervention can't work, rather than proof this specific version of it didn't.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One good thing. Gail Youngdale watched Alzheimer's take her own mother, and then got the diagnosis herself.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Instead of waiting it out, she enrolled in a clinical trial for lecanemab — the plaque-clearing therapy. The 9 spots of amyloid plaque doctors had found in her brain are gone now. Her decline's stopped.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And there's a second half to this story that has nothing to do with the drug.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: At a high school reunion, decades after both had lost their spouses, she reconnected with Phil Mercer — a boy she'd known back in junior high. They got married.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's the kind of story that doesn't need us to add anything to it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: No commentary required. Sometimes the story's just good, full stop — no counter-take needed, no risk to underwrite, nobody left holding the bag. That's the show — Monday, September 7. We'll see you tomorrow.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Have a good one.
